Symptom Guide: Headache
General health awareness information — not a diagnosis
Symptom Overview
A headache is pain or discomfort felt in the head, forehead, or back of the neck. It is one of the most common health complaints and happens to almost everyone at some point. Most headaches are mild and go away on their own or with simple rest and care. Some headaches, however, can be a sign that the body needs medical attention. This guide explains common reasons for headache, safe self-care steps, and warning signs that mean a person should see a health worker or doctor without delay.
Possible Common Causes
There are many possible reasons a person may get a headache. This list is only to build awareness — it does not diagnose any illness. A trained health worker or doctor is needed to find the real cause.
Not drinking enough water (dehydration), especially in hot weather
Skipping meals or low blood sugar
Lack of sleep or a disturbed sleep pattern
Stress, worry, or mental tiredness
Long hours in strong sun or working outdoors in heat
Eye strain from reading, screens, or uncorrected eyesight problems
Tight neck or shoulder muscles from poor posture
Fever, cold, cough, sinus block, or other infections
High blood pressure
Overuse of painkillers or too much tea, coffee, or tobacco, or suddenly stopping them
Migraine or tension-type headache, which are common and often repeat over time
Self-Care Advice
For a mild, ordinary headache, the following simple steps can help. These are general measures, not treatment for a specific disease.
Rest in a quiet, cool, and dimly lit room
Drink water or oral rehydration solution (ORS), especially in hot weather or after sweating a lot
Eat on time; do not stay hungry for long periods
Gently massage the forehead, neck, or shoulders
Sleep for a proper number of hours and keep a regular sleep routine
Reduce screen time and rest the eyes periodically
Avoid strong sun exposure between late morning and mid-afternoon; use a cloth or umbrella for head cover if going out
A mild, common painkiller such as paracetamol may be used occasionally by adults as per the instructions on the package, only if there is no other medical condition or ongoing medicine that could interact with it
Avoid overusing painkillers, as taking them too often can itself cause more headaches
When to Seek Medical Attention
Most headaches are not dangerous, but certain signs need urgent medical care. Go to the nearest health centre, hospital, or call an emergency number right away if any of the following occur:
Sudden, very severe headache, unlike any headache felt before
Headache with high fever, stiff neck, or a rash
Headache after a fall, blow to the head, or accident
Headache with confusion, slurred speech, weakness, or numbness on one side of the body
Headache with fainting, seizures (fits), or loss of consciousness
Headache with repeated vomiting, blurred or double vision
Headache that keeps getting worse over hours or days and does not improve with rest
Headache in a pregnant woman, especially with swelling of hands or face, or vision changes
Headache in a young child, elderly person, or someone with a known illness such as high blood pressure or diabetes
Any headache accompanied by very high body temperature, dizziness, and heavy sweating during hot weather, which may indicate heat-related illness and needs prompt medical evaluation
Odisha-Specific Notes
During Odisha's summer and heat-wave months, headache is commonly reported alongside dizziness, weakness, nausea, or fainting due to heat exhaustion or heat stroke. Health authorities advise avoiding outdoor work between 12 noon and 3 pm during heat-wave alerts, drinking water regularly even without feeling thirsty, and using ORS or homemade drinks such as buttermilk, lemon water, or coconut water to stay hydrated. If headache during hot weather is accompanied by very high body temperature, confusion, or fainting, this is treated as a medical emergency — seek help immediately or call the state emergency helplines (108 or 102). Local Anganwadi centres, sub-centres, and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) under Odisha's public health system can provide first-line care and guidance, and can refer a person onward if needed.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the National Health Mission (NHM), and heat-wave health advisories issued for Odisha by state health authorities and the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority (OSDMA). It reflects general awareness information current as of 2026 and does not cite any single source verbatim.
World Health Organization (WHO) – who.int
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India – mohfw.gov.in
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) – icmr.gov.in
National Health Mission (NHM) – nhm.gov.in
Odisha State Disaster Management Authority (OSDMA) – heat wave advisories
Government of Odisha, Health & Family Welfare Department
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
